analysis.one_liner: Reinstates and broadens the federal ban on assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee from February 2007 until that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring back the federal assault weapons ban that expired in 2004, with a broader definition covering specific rifles, pistols, and shotguns by name and by features like detachable magazines and pistol grips. It would require all future transfers of these weapons to go through a licensed dealer with a background check, ban large-capacity ammunition magazines, ban importing them, make it a crime to sell these weapons to juveniles, and require the Justice Department to publish a yearly report on crimes involving these guns. Existing owners could keep their weapons, but selling one would require going through a dealer.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by gun violence, and law enforcement officers, who were the intended beneficiaries of a smaller pool of military-style firearms and large-capacity magazines on the street. Existing owners could keep their guns.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates for ten years the criminal ban on semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices that Congress let expire in 2004 [S2][S3].
Requires that transfers of covered weapons go only through a licensed dealer or a law enforcement agency, which subjects them to dealer background-check procedures [S2][S3].
Makes it unlawful to transfer any assault weapon with a large-capacity ammunition feeding device, with penalties of up to 10 years in prison, and bans importing such devices [S3].
Directs the Attorney General to keep a public record of covered weapons used in crimes and report annually to Congress, and to ban transfers of these weapons to juveniles [S2][S3].
Grandfathers weapons already lawfully owned, so current owners would not have to surrender them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers that make the listed rifles, pistols, and shotguns, licensed dealers who would have to handle every private transfer through their shops, and owners who could no longer sell their guns privately without going through a dealer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: The named-weapon and feature-based definitions are broad: semiautomatic rifles with a detachable magazine and any one common feature such as a pistol grip or threaded barrel are covered, which sweeps in many ordinary hunting and sporting rifles, not just military-style guns [S3].
Existing owners could keep their weapons, but every future sale would have to run through a licensed dealer, adding cost and paperwork for private transfers [S3].

Researchers did not agree the 1994-2004 ban had reduced gun crime, since the grandfathered stock of banned weapons and pre-2004 magazines remained in circulation; opponents argued the bill restricted lawful owners without clear public-safety gains. The bill's findings section relies on law-enforcement testimony rather than settled evidence [S3].

The Attorney General would get discretion to decide which military-design firearms are 'not particularly suitable for sporting purposes,' which critics saw as an open-ended expansion of banned weapons [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restrict a category of firearms whose use in high-profile shootings drives public support for bans, and it pairs the ban with traceability reporting and a magazine import ban. The cost falls on manufacturers, dealers, and owners of covered guns, and the broad feature-based definition means more guns are covered than the name 'assault weapon' suggests. The biggest honest question is effectiveness: with weapons and magazines already in circulation grandfathered in, the near-term effect on violence would depend on how quickly the banned stock cycles out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2007, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and no action was ever taken on it before that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy introduced the bill on February 13, 2007, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
On March 19, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it stayed [S5].
The bill had 67 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
No subcommittee vote, committee vote, or House floor vote was ever held, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, dealers, and owners of the covered rifles, pistols, and shotguns are better off, because the ban never came to a vote, let alone became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and owners of covered weapons

industries.note: The bill bans a long list of named rifles, pistols, and shotguns plus feature-based definitions, and bans large-capacity magazines, cutting off legal civilian sales of those products [S3].
They would lose private-transfer business being routed through their shops under the bill, but they also gain mandated transaction fees and paperwork for every sale of a covered weapon [S3].
The bill makes it unlawful to import or bring into the United States any large-capacity ammunition feeding device [S3].
